book_intro: The book of Jeremiah is set during the politically tumultuous times following the fall of the Assyrians and the rise of the Babylonians. During Jeremiah's life, several groups of Judeans were deported to Babylon and the temple was destroyed. Though the precise boundaries of Judea and the surrounding regions during this period are difficult to determine, they likely resembled those that previously existed under Assyrian rule, with the exception that Edom (Idumea) was now the area formerly belonging to southern Judah.
chapter_intro: Jeremiah’s Struggles with God and Judah.

passages.title: Jeremiah’s Struggles with God and Judah.
passages.text: As the nation faces invasion, Jeremiah struggles to serve God faithfully. He is surprised by opposition (11:1–12:17), stunned over feeling betrayed by God (13:1–15:21), renewed by God (16:1–17:18), burdened by opposition (17:19–18:23), and prepared to continue serving (19:1–20:18).

notes.text: I brought them out. God alone deserves credit for the exodus (Ex. 20:1–2). iron furnace. Egypt forced Israel to make bricks (Ex. 5:1–21). My people . . . your God underscores the relational nature of the covenant. For similar language, see Deut. 4:20 and 1 Kings 8:51.
conspiracy. Against Yahweh, to serve other gods (v. 10).
iniquities of their forefathers. Idolatry committed with the golden calf (Ex. 32:1–6), Baal (Judg. 2:11–15), and other false gods (Jer. 7:16–20; 8:2).
disaster. The nation’s destruction by Babylon.
Superstitious polytheism (worship of many gods) fills Jerusalem. Baal. See 2:8.
do not pray. God will not grant Jeremiah’s prayer for a delay in punishment (see 7:16; 14:11).
Green olive tree signifies fruitfulness and economic prosperity (Ps. 52:8). great tempest. The storm of invasion (see Ezek. 1:24).
God reveals a plot against Jeremiah, who commits his future to his deliverer.
Anathoth. Jeremiah’s hometown (1:1). Do not prophesy. Even Jeremiah’s old friends hate his message, for it exposes their sins. They prefer false prophets (5:12–13).
God will protect his word and his prophet. sword . . . famine. Babylon’s attacks and natural disaster will overwhelm Anathoth.
